title: Supabase (GoTrue sessions, PostgREST, Postgres) on a local stack
summary: An app whose users sign in with Supabase Auth and whose data is Postgres behind row-level security, run as a local `supabase start` copy. Init probes the app or PostgREST itself with each user's access token, judges row-level security's empty answers by their body, and decides the backend row from the Postgres write-ahead log, which the app cannot edit.

gatewayHeaders.why: Supabase's gateway (Kong) may want the project's anon key in an apikey header beside the user's bearer token. The local CLI stack accepts the user's token alone; a gateway that answers 401 without the header needs the src/ gateway-header hook (connectors/README.md).

refusals.means: PostgREST answers a row that row-level security hides with 200 and an empty list, never 403.
A single-row read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object, or an app route over .maybeSingle()) of a hidden row answers null.
An UPDATE or DELETE that row-level security filters changes zero rows and answers 204 (or 200 []), never 403.
A signed-out request to an app route, or PostgREST without a valid token where anon has no grant.
An app route that checks ownership itself.
An app route that hides another tenant's record.
PostgREST's single-object read of a hidden row (vnd.pgrst.object with zero rows).

observers.why: The Postgres write-ahead log, read through a temporary logical slot the observer's own session holds. The app cannot remove a committed change from it, so a window with no change to the record decides the backend row (custody observer-held, for an absence only).

unloggedTables.why: pg_net's request queue is unlogged, so the WAL never carries it and every window reads partial (table-not-in-wal). init --stack never ignores it: it reports whether the migrations and the live catalog show pg_net used, and windows stay partial until its requests are observed on the wire (an egress recorder under a confined run).

setup: A local `supabase start` stack runs Postgres with wal_level=logical already; check with `select current_setting('wal_level')`.
Create the observer's own role once, as supabase_admin on the local copy only: CREATE ROLE scopehaven_wal LOGIN REPLICATION PASSWORD '<a generated test password>'; (it needs no SELECT on any table).
Put SCOPEHAVEN_TARGET_<APP>_DB_WAL=scopehaven_wal:<that password> in the observer env file (--observer-env), never in the identities' env file or the app's .env.

With pg_cron installed, also GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA cron TO scopehaven_wal; GRANT SELECT ON cron.job TO scopehaven_wal; ALTER ROLE scopehaven_wal BYPASSRLS; (cron.job has row-level security, so without BYPASSRLS the role sees only its own jobs) so init's report can say whether a job calls pg_net (the queue stays watched either way).

observers.why: Reads the app's rows before and after a check. The app can write those rows, so it decides allowed-use controls and FAILs, never a boundary pass on its own.
setup: Create a read-only role as supabase_admin on the local copy: CREATE ROLE scopehaven_read LOGIN BYPASSRLS PASSWORD '<a generated test password>'; GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO scopehaven_read; GRANT SELECT ON <the observed tables> TO scopehaven_read;

observers.why: Supabase Auth and app mail pointed at a loopback SMTP sink (in place of Inbucket or Mailpit), so mail the app sends is seen on the wire.
The app's outbound API base URLs (model, payments, webhooks) pointed at the loopback egress recorder.

backendRow.title: The foreign record's row is not changed by the read (Postgres write-ahead log)

supabaseRules.needs: An actor capture installed by a superuser on the disposable copy (integrations/observers/pg-actor.mjs). Init drafts the block; installing it is the operator's step, since it changes the copy's schema.

reset.note: Re-applies the migrations and seed to the local copy. Never against a hosted project.

limits: Local `supabase start` copies only, on loopback. A hosted Supabase project is never probed or observed.
The backend row decides that the foreign record's row was not written during the read. Postgres does not log reads, so no observer here shows the row was never loaded.
The apikey gateway header is declared but sent only once the gateway-header hook lands in src/; until then a gateway that requires it reads 401 on every row.
Write checks, the RLS zero-row rule and actor capture are drafted, not run, by init.
